Upvoat for you because that's an incredibly difficult question to answer. There is no such thing really.
Sorting out obvious tabloid trash is a good first step, but by no means sufficient. You have to really examine each issue individually with it's source. For popular news you have to heavily apply stakeholder analysis. So who's packaging the information (Obviously Russia Today is a bad bad source for information on Ukrainian politics), and what their source information was (did they receive their information from detailed reports, (who's reports again?) or is it the same inquisitive back alley hobo CNN is always quoting with "Some people question....")

Ultimately if you really want to be properly informed on a topic you have to go beyond popular media and delve into the world of dry analysis reports, unfortunately these are sometimes difficult or impossible to find. Example: If someone in Ukraine complains that the Russians aren't playing nice the president doesn't pick up the New York Post to figure out where they are, he requests packaged intelligence from the National Reconnaissance Office and perhaps, for this example, allied assets but again with a grain of salt. If you want to know if there's an increase of crime as a function of immigration, you don't go to Fox News you look at specific FBI or DOJ reports on the subject and cross reference them with reports from independent agencies. (Again checking to see who financed the reports and why and even then you're not completely sure their methodology was sound.) It's hard work and it sucks and it may be beyond the scope of what people look for with "news". What you do not do is consult obviously biased sources, at a minimum you can do a passing check for objectivity on the subject.
